title: Random-matrix reduction in projective quantum mechanics
abstract: We develop a state-space geometric framework for measurement, classicality, and quantum paradoxes, based on one dynamical conjecture. Classical configuration space and classical phase space for a mechanical system arise as distinguished submanifolds of projective quantum state space. On these submanifolds, the Fubini--Study geometry induces Euclidean classical geometry, and the tangent component of Schrödinger evolution reproduces Newtonian dynamics. Within this framework, interactions with measuring devices and environments are described by random-matrix dynamics on projective state space, generated by matrices drawn from the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble. We show that this random-matrix dynamics yields isotropic diffusion, giving Born-rule transition probabilities in microscopic measurements and stabilizing classical behavior in macroscopic systems. We further argue that the random-matrix conjecture is not an independent ad hoc assumption: under natural translation-invariance assumptions on the distribution of state-space steps originating on the classical submanifold, the unitary lift of homogeneous and isotropic Brownian motion on that submanifold is uniquely given by the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble, up to scale and an irrelevant scalar part. The resulting framework provides a unitary account of measurement and the quantum-to-classical transition and, if accepted, offers a dynamical resolution of standard quantum paradoxes.
summary: The paper proposes that quantum mechanics can be understood by viewing classical reality as specific, localized submanifolds embedded within the full projective quantum state space. Measurement and environmental interaction are modeled unitarily via random-matrix dynamics (GUE), which forces stochastic diffusion leading to Born probabilities and stabilizing macroscopic systems into predictable Newtonian trajectories.
main_problem: To develop a unified, geometrically consistent framework that resolves foundational quantum mechanics problems like measurement, the origin of the Born rule, and the quantum-to-classical transition.
main_result: The framework successfully embeds classical dynamics (Newtonian motion) as distinguished submanifolds within the projective quantum state space, while environmental interactions are modeled by random-matrix dynamics yielding isotropic diffusion.
method: It employs a geometric approach, identifying classical spaces with low-resolution equivalence classes on the projective state manifold. Measurement and environment coupling are modeled using Random Matrix Theory (GUE) to enforce unitary stochastic evolution.
model_or_system: The system is quantum mechanics evolving in the projective Hilbert space ($	ext{CPL}^2$). Classical dynamics emerge when the state is restricted to localized submanifolds ($M_\sigma^3$) whose geometry is Euclidean, yielding Newtonian equations via the tangent component of the Schrödinger flow.
key_observables: Born-rule transition probabilities (microscopic); Stroboscopic Newtonian trajectories (macroscopic); Equivalence classes defining measurement outcomes.
important_parameters: Localization parameter $\sigma$ (related to measurement resolution); Planck's constant ($\hbar$); Random Matrix Ensemble (GUE).
main_assumptions: The central assumption is the Random-Matrix Conjecture, positing that environmental interactions are unitarily equivalent to random matrices drawn from the GUE. It also assumes classicality arises from finite-resolution coarse-graining.
figures_summary: Not specified in notes; figures likely illustrate the geometric embedding of classical manifolds within the projective state space and the stochastic nature of measurement paths.
paper_structure: The paper builds by first establishing the geometric embedding of classical phase/configuration spaces as submanifolds. It then introduces the Random-Matrix Conjecture to model environmental coupling, showing this leads to isotropic diffusion (Born rule). Finally, it synthesizes these elements to provide a unitary account of measurement and the quantum-to-classical transition.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly abstract yet potentially unifying geometric mechanism for solving foundational problems in QM, linking stochastic processes (Brownian motion/GUE) directly to the emergence of classical determinism within a strictly unitary framework.
